references.text: Joshua 16:1 mentions the road from Jericho up toward the mountains near Jerusalem, the same route that the man in the parable traveled down—from Jerusalem to Jericho.
In Judges 9:25 men lie in ambush on mountain peaks to rob passersby, which recalls the robbers who attacked the man on the road.
Hosea 6:9 (book ID 28) refers to bands of priests who lurk along the way and commit crimes—a parallel to the robbers who assaulted the traveler.
Jesus predicts his own suffering in Jerusalem—he will be handed over, mistreated, and killed. The parable of the man beaten half to death can be seen in light of Jesus' own fate.
Jesus goes up to Jerusalem, the same road between Jerusalem and Jericho that forms the background for the parable of the good Samaritan.
Paul mentions dangers from robbers among his sufferings as an apostle, which recalls the brutality of the robbery in Jesus' parable.
The preceding context where a lawyer asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus responds with a question that leads into the parable of the good Samaritan.
The Samaritan who shows mercy to the half-dead man constitutes the direct follow-up to the consequences of the robbery in verse 30.
